principles.name: Client Service
principles.description: Lead with a service mindset; earn clients' trust and exceed their expectations by understanding their goals. Clients' interests come first.
evidence_signals: Names the client or internal user and what they actually needed
Went beyond the request and shows the effect for the client
Kept the client informed when something went wrong

principles.name: Partnership
principles.description: Prioritize collaboration and the strength of the team over individual credit.
evidence_signals: Worked across teams or desks to deliver something no one team could
Gives credit to others while being clear about own part
Helped a colleague succeed at a cost to own time

principles.name: Integrity
principles.description: Hold to the highest ethical standards, be transparent, and own mistakes; follow controls even under pressure.
evidence_signals: Raised a risk or mistake early, including own mistake
Followed change control or compliance rules under deadline pressure
Explains a decision openly rather than hiding trade-offs

principles.name: Excellence
principles.description: Strive for exceptional performance and superior results; high standards for correctness and detail.
evidence_signals: Shows attention to detail and testing, especially on edge cases
Set a higher bar than required and explains the result
Learns quickly and improves after feedback

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: Two or three coding problems graded on hidden tests. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Recorded video interview
rounds.notes: Mainly for campus and early-career hires: a few recorded behavioral and motivation questions with a short time to answer.

rounds.name: Technical screen
rounds.notes: One or two live calls, usually a CoderPad coding problem plus a resume discussion. Coding part not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Superday: coding
rounds.notes: One or two coding rounds, easy to medium difficulty; correctness and edge cases matter. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Superday: system design
rounds.notes: Design with a correctness and auditability focus, such as market-data ingestion, positions or order management. Java and SDLC questions are common.

rounds.name: Superday: resume and behavioral
rounds.notes: Why Goldman, why this division, teamwork and past projects in depth.

rounds.name: Team-match conversation
rounds.notes: Some candidates meet one or two specific teams after the Superday to check stack and team fit.

rounds.name: Managing director conversation
rounds.notes: Short final conversation on motivation and fit; may include an unexpected technical question.

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: Coding plus probability and math questions for strats and quant roles. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical screen
rounds.notes: Probability, statistics and a discussion of a past model or project.

rounds.name: Superday: probability and modelling
rounds.notes: Probability puzzles reasoned aloud, plus modelling questions tied to pricing or risk.

rounds.name: Superday: behavioral
rounds.notes: Motivation, teamwork with traders or bankers, and handling pressure.

question_patterns.theme: Why Goldman and why this division
question_patterns.pattern: Why the candidate wants this firm and this business area, tied to what the division's engineers actually build
A time the candidate worked with others under a tight deadline and how they kept the team together
A mistake or production issue the candidate caused or found, how they raised it, and what changed afterwards
A time the candidate dealt with a demanding client or internal user and delivered what they needed
A time the candidate disagreed with a teammate or senior colleague about an approach and how it was resolved
Design a trading-related service (positions, market data, orders) with focus on ordering, idempotency, reconciliation and audit
Explain a core language or software-process concept (collections, concurrency, testing, release controls) and when it matters
A probability or expected-value puzzle reasoned aloud, with conditioning shown step by step
Walk through the most significant project on the resume: the candidate's part, the hardest technical choice and the result

sample_questions.question: Why do you want to work at Goldman Sachs, and why in this particular division?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Be specific and sincere. Link your interests to what the division's engineers build (for example trading platforms, risk systems, consumer or asset-management technology) and to the firm's values, such as client service and partnership. Mention a concrete product, talk or person you learned from, and how your skills fit. Show that you understand engineering here sits close to the business. Pitfalls: generic prestige or pay answers, or not knowing what the division does.

strong_signals: Names a specific platform or business problem
Connects own skills to that work

sample_questions.question: How would you design a service that ingests market data and keeps trading positions up to date?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify scale, latency and correctness needs first. Sketch ingestion from feeds, a durable log or queue, a position service and a store, plus a query API. Then spend most time on correctness: message ordering, duplicates and gaps, idempotent updates, sequence numbers, and reconciling positions against an end-of-day source after failures. Cover audit trails and monitoring. Pitfalls: optimizing only for scale, or ignoring what happens when messages are lost or replayed.

watch_outs: Pure scale talk with no correctness story

sample_questions.question: Design the main classes for a simple banking system with customers, accounts and credit cards. How do they relate, and how would you keep balances correct?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start from use cases (open account, deposit, withdraw, transfer, card payment). Propose classes such as Customer, Account (with subtypes), Card and Transaction, and explain the relationships and which object owns which behavior. Keep balances correct with an append-only transaction record, atomic transfers, validation rules and clear handling of concurrent updates. Mention where a design pattern helps, for example a strategy for fee or interest rules. Pitfalls: a class list with no behavior, or balances updated with no audit trail.

looking_for: Clean object modelling from use cases
How correctness of money is protected
strong_signals: Sensible use of a design pattern

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time something you were responsible for failed. What did you do next?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real failure with consequences, for example a release that broke something. Own your part without blaming others. Explain how quickly you raised it, how you limited the impact, and the root cause. Describe the fix and what you changed (tests, checks, process) so it cannot recur, and what you learned. Pitfalls: a fake failure, blaming others, or no prevention step.

strong_signals: Raised the issue quickly and openly
Added a test or control so it cannot recur
watch_outs: A failure that was not really yours

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you worked on a team under a tight deadline. What was your role and how did it turn out?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set up the deadline and why it mattered. Be clear about your own role and decisions, how the team split work, and how you handled friction or a teammate who was stuck. Show the result and what you would do differently. Pitfalls: only 'we', or a story where the team succeeded despite poor collaboration.

looking_for: Your own role inside the team
strong_signals: Clear split of work and own decisions

sample_questions.question: You roll a fair die until a six appears. What is the expected sum of all the rolls, including the six?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Reason aloud. The number of rolls is geometric with mean 6. Each roll before the six is uniform on 1 to 5 with mean 3, and there are on average 5 such rolls, giving 15; add the final six for an expected total of 21. Cross-check with Wald's identity: 6 expected rolls times 3.5 per roll is also 21. Check the answer for sense. Pitfalls: guessing, or forgetting that pre-six rolls cannot be six.

watch_outs: Ignoring that earlier rolls exclude six

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Delivers well-defined features with guidance; writes correct, tested code and learns the business domain.
Owns components or services within a team, designs features and works directly with business users.
Leads design for a system or small team, owns delivery and production risk, and mentors associates and analysts.
Sets technical direction for a platform or group of teams and represents engineering to business leaders.
Builds and maintains pricing, risk or analytics models with traders or bankers, owning their correctness.

persona.tone: Professional, polite and businesslike; more formal than a tech company
persona.pace: Brisk; Superday interviews run back to back with little small talk
persona.pushback_style: Checks precision: asks about edge cases, failure handling and 'why this firm'; pushes for specifics on own role
persona.closing_style: Leaves a few minutes for questions; no feedback given

case_style.notes: No business case round for engineering roles. Closest equivalents are correctness-focused system design for trading systems and probability or estimation puzzles for strats.

sources.title: What is the Goldman Sachs interview process like (Design Gurus)

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the four values are official; principle weights are our estimate.
loop_structure: no official Goldman page describes the engineering loop; round count (3 to 6 Superday interviews) and HireVue length vary by source, division and year.
bar_by_level: Analyst, Associate, VP and MD titles are public; the scope text is our summary, not a published ladder.
persona: based on candidate reports, not an official description.
scoring_weights: no public source; derived from the emphasis on correctness and teamwork in reports.
loop_structure: the data_ml (strats) loop comes from one prep guide.
